title: Smoke and CO alarms: loud horn, cell and sensors
summary: Every building has smoke alarms. Each holds a very loud piezo horn with its driver circuit, a battery (sometimes a sealed 10-year lithium cell) and a sensor. Ionisation types hold a tiny radioactive source: leave its chamber sealed and keep it out of reach.

steps.text: Twist the alarm off its ceiling base. Hard-wired alarms have a plug on a short lead: unplug it.
steps.warn: Hard-wired alarms run on mains. If the grid could come back, switch off the circuit before touching the base wiring.

steps.text: Read the label on the back. A radiation symbol or the words "americium" or "radioactive" means an ionisation alarm. "Photoelectric" or "optical" means a light-based sensor. CO alarms say carbon monoxide.
Take the battery out: a 9 V battery or AA cells pop out of a door. Sealed 10-year alarms have the cell soldered or tabbed inside the case.
Open the case: undo any screws, then work a flat screwdriver around the seam and pop the clips.
Sealed lithium cell: cut its two tabs one at a time, taping each end. It is a 3 V or 3.6 V primary cell. Do not try to recharge it.
steps.warn: Cutting both tabs at once shorts the cell. A shorted lithium cell gets hot and can vent.

steps.text: Ionisation alarm: find the sensing chamber, a small metal can with slots or mesh, soldered to the board. Leave it closed. If you want the board, cut the board around the chamber or desolder the horn instead.
steps.warn: Never open, crush, burn or file the chamber. The source is safe sealed but harmful if its dust is breathed in or swallowed.

steps.text: Photoelectric alarm: pry off the black plastic maze cover in the middle. Inside is an infrared LED and a light sensor facing across the maze. Keep them on the board or desolder them as a pair.
Keep the horn: a flat piezo disc in a round plastic cavity, usually with 3 wires or pins. Keep it on the board: the board already drives it from 9 V. Pressing the test button sounds it.
CO alarms: keep the horn and battery. Leave the sensor cell sealed; it wears out after 5–10 years and holds a little electrolyte.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The horn and its board.** A whole alarm board is a ready-made very loud siren (about 85 dB at 3 m) that runs on a 9 V battery. Bridge the test button with a switch, a tripwire contact or a door contact and you have an alarm for a gate, a door or a chicken run (see build_perimeter_alarm).
- **Batteries.** 9 V batteries, AA cells, or sealed 3–3.6 V lithium primaries that often have years of charge left.
- **IR LED and light sensor pair.** From photoelectric alarms. A beam-break or smoke sensor.
- **Test button, small switches.**

## About the radioactive source

Ionisation alarms hold a tiny amount of americium-241, usually about 1 microcurie (37 kBq) or less, sealed in foil inside the metal chamber. It gives off alpha particles, which can't get through skin or even a sheet of paper. Outside your body it is close to harmless. Inside your body it is not. So:

- Leave the chamber shut.
- Don't let children play with it.
- If you collect many, store them together in a sealed metal tin away from living and food areas, and label it.
- If a chamber is damaged, wet a paper towel, pick it up without touching it, seal it in a bag and a tin, and wash your hands.

## Variations

- Many alarms since the 2010s are photoelectric only and have no radioactive source.
- Combination smoke and CO alarms have both sensors.
- Hard-wired alarms add a small mains power supply and an interconnect wire that lets one alarm trigger the others.
- Commercial buildings use addressable detectors wired to a fire panel; those have no horn of their own (see fire_panel).

## What to leave

- The CO sensor cell and the ionisation chamber.
- The plastic case, unless you need a ready-made project box.
